name: Clinical Decision Support
title: Clinical Decision Support
answer: Clinical decision support in this part of the atlas covers software that turns clinical documentation and ambient conversation into structured suggestions, alerts, and documentation aids for clinicians. It includes tools that listen to patient encounters, extract problems and orders, and compare them against guidelines or patient history. The focus is on support for diagnosis, treatment, and documentation rather than autonomous care. These systems sit between the electronic health record and the clinician, aiming to reduce documentation burden while flagging possible omissions or risks.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Clinical decision support in this part of the atlas covers software that turns clinical documentation and ambient conversation into structured suggestions, alerts, and documentation aids for clinicians. It includes tools that listen to patient encounters, extract problems and orders, and compare them against guidelines or patient history. The focus is on support for diagnosis, treatment, and documentation rather than autonomous care. These systems sit between the electronic health record and the clinician, aiming to reduce documentation burden while flagging possible omissions or risks.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most clinical decision support tools run inside or alongside the electronic health record, often as cloud services that receive audio, text, or structured data from the care setting. Ambient systems rely on secure microphones and speech-to-text pipelines, while documentation tools may use application programming interfaces to read and write notes. Compute is typically hosted by the vendor or the health system, with strict access controls and encryption for protected health information. Some deployments run on local servers to meet data residency or reliability requirements.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by combining speech recognition, natural language processing, and clinical knowledge bases. Ambient systems transcribe the conversation, identify speakers, and map utterances to medical concepts such as symptoms, medications, and procedures. A language model or rules engine then drafts a note or proposes orders, which a clinician must review and sign. Structured data extracted from the note can be checked against drug interactions, care gaps, or billing requirements before it enters the record.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: These tools raise direct questions about patient consent, data retention, and who is responsible when a suggestion is wrong or missed. Recordings and transcripts are sensitive health data, so access, audit logs, and deletion policies matter as much as model accuracy. Product liability and wrongful death claims against AI companies are an active area tracked by this atlas, and clinical decision support vendors face regulatory scrutiny when their output influences care. Provenance is critical: a clinician needs to know whether a suggestion came from a guideline, a learned pattern, or a transcription error.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward ambient systems that draft notes and orders in real time with less clinician prompting, and toward decision support that pulls from the full patient record rather than a single encounter. Expect tighter integration with clinical guidelines, prior authorizations, and quality measures, but also more pressure to show that these tools improve outcomes without adding alert fatigue. As models become more capable, the boundary between documentation aid and diagnostic suggestion will blur, which will force clearer rules about validation and clinician override.
